title: The separation-of-powers critique of interpreting an agency’s own rules
shortTitle: The separation-of-powers critique of interpreting an agency’s own rules
summary: The Kisor notes contrast the argument that combining rulewriting and authoritative interpretation encourages agency overreach with defenses of interpretation as part of executing a statutory program.
notes:
Justice Scalia’s separate opinion in Decker, reproduced in the notes, argues that letting an agency authoritatively interpret its own language joins prescription and interpretation and encourages vague rules followed by potentially retroactive clarification. The notes identify John Manning’s earlier academic version of this structural critique. This is an attributed challenge to Auer, not the holding of the Kisor majority. (Printed 1001–1002.)

Sunstein and Vermeule’s response, as characterized by the editors, rejects the premise that agency interpretation unlawfully expands power. Kagan’s four-Justice Kisor discussion treats agency activities taking legislative or adjudicative form as exercises of executive authority under a statutory plan and emphasizes the courts’ retained reviewing role. Gorsuch disputes the statutory and constitutional sufficiency of those limits. The disagreement involves both institutional power and the practical consequences of interpretation without notice and comment. (Printed 994, 997–1002.)

The final express-delegation hypothetical asks whether an agency could write a regulation authorizing later interpretive rules to define its terms. That question tests whether an explicit instruction resolves only an implied-delegation problem or also confronts limits arising from the APA and constitutional structure. The source poses the problem and leaves the answer open.
